claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by gradient heat treatment will produce a controlled gradient nanostructure in a high-entropy alloy.
The resulting gradient nanostructure will synergistically improve strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to a homogeneous microstructure.
Severe plastic deformation will produce a nanocrystalline surface layer.
Gradient heat treatment will establish a graded transition from a nanocrystalline surface to a coarse-grained interior.
A controlled temperature gradient up to about 600°C with moderate strain rates can preserve the gradient microstructure.
Over-annealing can erase the gradient and cause the proposed method to fail.
Strain rates that are too high or too low can cause the proposed method to fail.
Poor alloy phase stability can prevent the proposed improvements.
The processing route will create a gradient in grain size and phase fraction from a nanostructured region to a coarser-grained core.
The graded microstructure will promote beneficial interfacial effects.
The nanocrystalline outer layer will increase yield strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The coarse-grained inner region will retain ductility.
The gradient structure will induce strain-gradient plasticity.
Strain-gradient plasticity will increase fracture resistance.
The gradient structure will permit local modulation of Young's modulus and thereby harmonize stiffness with toughness.
Gradient-structured samples will exhibit at least a 15–20% improvement in yield strength over homogeneous controls.
Gradient-structured samples will exhibit a 10–15% increase in ductility over homogeneous controls.
Gradient-structured samples will exhibit measurable enhancements in Young's modulus and fracture toughness over homogeneous controls.
Direct empirical evidence for gradient nanostructuring techniques in high-entropy alloys is limited.
